title: Date and situation
short: Written on 27 May 1916, while Thomas was an army map-reading instructor considering a commission and service in France.
body: Edward Thomas (1878-1917) enlisted in the Artists Rifles in July 1915. In 1916 he was a map-reading instructor at Hare Hall camp in Essex, and the poem, dated 27 May 1916 on the manuscript, was written as he moved toward applying for a commission that would take him to France. He was killed at Arras on 9 April 1917. The poem first appeared in Poems (1917) under his pseudonym 'Edward Eastaway'. Its dialogue with a ploughman about whether to go to the war is therefore close to Thomas's own decision.

title: head-brass
short: The brass ornaments on the horses' harness or bridles, which catch the light as the plough team turns.
body: A 'team' is a pair or more of horses yoked to the plough. Horse brasses were polished brass ornaments fixed to the harness and bridle, and the 'head-brass' is the brass on the horses' heads. Its flash at each turn of the plough marks the poem's rhythm: the conversation happens in snatches each time the team comes round. The flashing light also hints, faintly, at military brass and the glint of war.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'brass, n.'

anchor: The lovers disappeared into the wood
title: The lovers
short: The lovers frame the poem, going into the wood at the start and coming out at the end: life continuing beside the war.
body: The lovers enter the wood in line 2 and come out in line 33, so they frame the whole conversation. They stand for love and the continuity of ordinary life, of generation, while the men talk of death. The image recalls Thomas Hardy's 'In Time of "The Breaking of Nations"' (1915), where a man harrowing clods and a pair of lovers outlast the 'dynasties' and wars of history. Critics have often compared the two poems.

sources.cite: Thomas Hardy, 'In Time of "The Breaking of Nations"' (1915; Moments of Vision, 1917)
Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)

title: the fallen elm
short: An elm felled by the blizzard, which would have been cleared if the ploughman's mate had not been killed.
body: The speaker sits in the branches of an elm brought down by a blizzard. The tree becomes the poem's quiet image of the war's effects on the home front: it lies where it fell because a farmworker who would have helped move it has been killed in France. The elm, a traditional feature of the English hedgerow landscape, has fallen like the soldiers.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)

title: fallow ... charlock
short: A fallow is land left unsown; charlock is wild mustard, a yellow-flowered weed of arable fields.
body: 'Fallow' is ploughed land left unsown for a season, here overgrown. Charlock (Sinapis arvensis, wild mustard) is a common yellow-flowered weed of cornfields, so the plough is turning a 'yellow square' of weed under. The square narrows with each turn, an image of time running out, and the precise botanical name is typical of Thomas, a prolific writer on the countryside before he turned to poetry.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'charlock'

title: the share ... screwed along the furrow
short: The share is the ploughshare, the blade that cuts the furrow; 'screwed' suggests the twisting effort of guiding the plough.
body: The ploughshare (share) is the iron blade at the front of the plough that cuts the soil; ploughmen scraped it clean of clinging earth at the end of each furrow. 'Screwed along the furrow' gives the effortful, twisting movement of man and team, and perhaps the ploughman screwing up his eyes. These technical details ground the poem in the real labour of the farm.

title: Blank verse and broken lines
short: Conversational blank verse with heavy enjambment and broken lines, influenced by Robert Frost's dramatic dialogues.
body: The poem is in unrhymed iambic pentameter, flexible enough to carry everyday speech. 'Once more.' is a half-line, completed after the gap by 'The blizzard felled the elm whose crest', and the visual break marks the pause before the talk begins. Thomas's close friend Robert Frost, whose North of Boston (1914) Thomas had reviewed, encouraged him to write verse that caught the 'sound of sense', the rhythm of the speaking voice, and the dialogues of this poem show that influence.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)
Matthew Spencer, ed., Elected Friends: Robert Frost and Edward Thomas to One Another (Handsel Books, 2003)

title: The blizzard
short: A great blizzard struck southern England at the end of March 1916, bringing down many trees.
body: Late March 1916 saw an exceptionally severe blizzard across southern England, which felled great numbers of trees, and the poem's date and details fit it. The ploughman ties the blizzard to the death of his mate in France 'the very night of the blizzard', so a home storm and a foreign death coincide. Natural and human catastrophe are both simply facts in his plain report.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)

title: One minute and an interval of ten
short: The talk is rationed by the plough's circuit: a minute of conversation each time the team turns, then ten of ploughing.
body: The rhythm of the dialogue follows the work: each time the team reaches the speaker's end of the field the ploughman stops for a word, then disappears for ten minutes along the furrow. The fragmented exchange that follows is therefore realistic. It also gives the poem a reticence typical of Thomas, since so much is left unsaid in the intervals.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)
Edward Thomas, The Collected Poems, ed. R. George Thomas (Oxford UP, 1978)

title: Have you been out?
short: 'Out' means out to the front in France; the speaker is in uniform but has not yet served overseas.
body: 'Been out' was the common wartime idiom for having served at the front. The ploughman's follow-up ('And don't want to, perhaps?') touches the question of willingness that Thomas himself was weighing in May 1916. The speaker's reply weighs injuries with grim levity: an arm he could spare, not a leg; and if he lost his head, he would want nothing more. The joke on 'lose my head' (be killed, but also panic) masks real fear.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)

title: Many lost? ... Only two teams
short: The village has lost many men; with only two teams working, the labour shortage of wartime farming shows.
body: 'Good few' is a dialect understatement meaning 'quite a lot'. With so many men gone, through volunteering and, from 1916, conscription under the Military Service Act, the farm works fewer teams. The ploughman's flat answers carry the scale of rural loss without any rhetoric. The exchange of short questions and one-word answers is spare, like the depleted village itself. Nobody names the dead.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)
Military Service Act 1916 (UK), introducing conscription

anchor: One of my mates is dead
title: One of my mates is dead
short: The ploughman's friend was killed on his second day in France, and that is why the elm still lies in the field.
body: The war enters the poem most directly in this plain sentence, and then at once returns to the fallen tree: if his mate had stayed, 'we should have moved the tree'. The logic links a death in France to a small change in an English field. Thomas's poetry often registers the war this way, obliquely, through its effects on the landscape at home.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)
Edward Thomas, The Collected Poems, ed. R. George Thomas (Oxford UP, 1978)

title: Another world ... If we could see all
short: The conditionals spiral: everything would be different; the ploughman adds a hesitant, providential 'better, though / If we could see all...'.
body: The speaker follows the ploughman's 'if' to its end: had the man stayed, he would not be sitting on the elm, and the world would be another world. The ploughman agrees it would be 'a better' world, then qualifies: 'If we could see all all might seem good.' The doubled 'all all' is deliberate. This is a countryman's version of providential consolation, that from a complete view everything would seem right, and its tentative 'might seem' leaves it uncertain. Critics differ on whether the line offers real consolation or a fatalism the poem does not share.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)
Edward Thomas, The Collected Poems, ed. R. George Thomas (Oxford UP, 1978)

title: for the last time
short: The plough team's last turn ends the scene, but 'last time' also anticipates death for the speaker (and for Thomas).
body: Literally, this is the last circuit the speaker watches before leaving. Readers who know Thomas's fate (killed at Arras less than a year later) hear an ominous second sense: a farewell to the English landscape. The lovers re-emerge at the same moment, so continuity (love) and ending (war, death) are juxtaposed in the poem's last movement. The poem gives no comment, leaving the reader to feel the doubleness.

sources.cite: Edward Thomas, The Annotated Collected Poems, ed. Edna Longley (Bloodaxe Books, 2008)
First World War Poetry Digital Archive (Oxford), manuscript of 'As the team's head-brass', dated 27 May 1916

title: clods crumble ... the stumbling team
short: The closing image of overturned earth suggests both continuing labour and the collapse of an old world.
body: The final lines show the earth crumbling and toppling behind the ploughshare, an image of renewal (ploughing prepares a crop) that also suggests destruction, even burial. The team is 'stumbling', no longer smooth. The scene recalls Hardy's 'In Time of "The Breaking of Nations"' ('Only a man harrowing clods'), where rural labour outlasts history. Thomas's version is less confident that the old rural order will survive the war.
